review_comments.author: Darrick J. Wong
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns that famfs doesn't handle overlapping mappings correctly, which could lead to kernel issues if not addressed.

review_comments.author: John Groves
review_comments.summary: Noted that famfs can already handle some edge cases, but also pointed out limitations and potential issues with reflinks and fsdax.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat, Aug 22, 2026, at 12:40 PM, Darrick J. Wong wrote:
> On Sat, Aug 22, 2026 at 12:18:58AM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
> > On Fri, Aug 21, 2026 at 05:07:28PM -0700, Darrick J. Wong wrote:
> > > 
> > > But what prevents a malicious program that is /not/ the famfs client
> > > software but has CAP_SYS_ADMIN from doing that?
> > > 
> > 
> > Such a program can already unmount famfs, rebind the device to
> > device_dax, and mmap the whole range directly. MAP_CREATE isn't
> > handing it reach it didn't have. 

Gregory is right, but also: this is possible with fuse too, since the log
needs to be played into a tree that the fuse server consumes - in order
to avoid searching the log (order n) on every lookup. 

> 
> Thinking about this a little more -- some random root process that
> accidentally tries to create/modify a directory tree on a famfs mount
> will just end up with fmap-less files that won't work for IO or
> mmapping.  That's dorky, but I think you're right that it's no big deal.

I've had users do that, and yes it's dorky but NBD.  It can be locked
down tighter by turning off FAMFS_OPT_CREATE except during 
log play etc., but the main thing is "don't do that: it won't harm the 
system, but it also it won't do what you want".

'famfs fsck' finds those, and the famfs cli can clean them up.

> 
> 
> A bigger question I just thought of is sharing cxlmem between files (aka
> reflink).  Is that allowed?  I could see a theoretical usecase for
> programs A and B wanting to share some cxlmem for communication or
> heartbeats whilst having their own /a and /b files for their private
> memory.  Probably you'd just create a /common file to do that and not
> map the same cxlmem page into /a and /b, right?

Famfs doesn't support reflinks - I don't think there's a use case.

There is a pcq.c and libpcq.c in the famfs user space specifically for
using file pairs as producer/consumer queues - one file contains the
fields written by the producer, the other contains the fields written
by the consumer. This use case works great, but without cache-coherent
cxl memory (which is coming but not here yet AFAIK) libpcq has to verify
message sequence numbers and checksums to avoid reading messages 
from stale cache lines (i.e. loaded before valid).

I do have CI that creates cross linked files, which are detected by 
'famfs fsck'. 

> 
> But having said that, the fsdax code /can/ support sharing between
> files, so I wonder if famfs is prepared either (a) to enable that
> sharing or (b) reject a mapping that would overlap with an existing
> mapping?  Things will go very badly in the kernel if famfs doesn't set
> up the dax_folio state correctly.
> 
> --D
> 

Last I checked, if cross linked files get created (as test_errors.sh in my
smoke test suite does), you trigger a WARN_ONCE from dax,
but otherwise it does no harm to the system.

Thanks,
John

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 1/8] mm/gup: break out gup_fill_pages() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out a helper function called gup_fill_pages() from the __get_user_pages() function in mm/gup.c. The new helper function fills pages[] and flushes each page's caches, which can then be used by other parts of the code that need to access multiple pages at once. This change is intended to improve maintainability and reduce code duplication, but does not introduce any functional changes. The patch also includes some minor code rearrangements to accommodate the new helper function.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 2/8] mm/gup: convert follow_page_mask() to return a long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch changes the return type of follow_page_mask() and its helper functions from struct page pointer to long. The function now returns 0, a negative errno, or 1 with the page stored in a new pages[0] slot. This allows the return value to carry a page count rather than a single struct page pointer.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 3/8] mm/gup: split follow_page_pte_commit() out of follow_page_pte()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the function follow_page_pte() into two separate functions: follow_page_pte_commit() and follow_page_pte(). The new function, follow_page_pte_commit(), handles the per-folio work of grabbing a reference to the page, making it accessible if necessary, marking it dirty or accessed if required, and filling in the pages array. This change allows for more granular control over when the safety checks and commit operations are applied, without changing any functionality. The patch is part of an ongoing effort to improve the Linux kernel's memory management subsystem.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) suggested that the function name and abstraction of follow_page_pte_commit() are not ideal, as it requires internal documentation to understand its purpose. He also proposed removing the pte parameter and instead passing in the result of pte_dirty(), and further suggested making the function capable of handling PMD/PUDs in addition to PTEs.
review_comments.raw_body:
If a function needs 4 lines of internal doc to understand what it does, then
maybe it's not the right function name or abstraction. :)

I don't particularly enjoy the "commit" terminology, it looses the detail of the
most important thing this function is supposed to to: grab a folio reference.

We're passing in the pte only to do a single pte_dirty(). If the helper is
actually what we want, likely we just just pass in the pte_dirty() directly and
remove all pte leftovers from the helper.

I'd assume that we'd want a function where we can similarly punch in a PMD/PUD
and have it do the same thing as well, instead of special-casing ptes.

Let me think about this some more, I might have to play with the code myself to
understand how this should all be cleaned up.

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that moving gup_fill_pages() outside the lock is necessary for PUD path, but noted it's a noop on most architectures except s390.

Author acknowledged a potential issue with marking the folio dirty and losing data written to the page, but did not commit to addressing it.
sentiment_signals: did not commit to addressing it
review_comments.raw_body:
It does more than grabbing, but if we want to
have the PUD path use this same function, we
will probably want to move the gup_fill_pages()
call to outside the lock.

At that point we'll be left with grabbing the
pages, and marking the folio dirty/accessed,
plus the arch_make_folio_accessible() call,
which seems to be a noop on anything but s390,
where it makes the page accessible to the
hypervisor (not sure when/why GUP needs this).

---

The page table dirty bits should ensure that we
don't lose any data written to the page, but not
marking the folio dirty might mess with dirty
balancing.

--

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: Author Rik Riel is addressing David's feedback about sub-folio dirty tracking, questioning whether marking folios dirty at GUP time is necessary and suggesting that it might be better to mark pages dirty when they are actually being written to. He plans to fix places in the kernel where this is not happening.
review_comments.raw_body:
Heh, now the filesystem people want sub-folio dirty
tracking, to reduce write amplification.

https://lore.kernel.org/all/aocFPRgqieScf_yo@pedro-suse.lan/

This makes me wonder that while your suggestion
makes sense for anonymous and tmpfs memory, we might
need something else for filesystem backed large
folios and get_user_pages?

Thinking about it some more, we are marking the 
folio dirty before (potentially long before) a write
is actually done.

Doesn't that give the flushing code time to clean
the page (by writing out content identical to what
is already on disk) before the actual dirtying of
the memory, through e.g. PTRACE_POKE is done?

Does the dirtying of folios and/or pages need to
be done when they are actually being written to,
and not at GUP time?

It looks like __access_remote_vm() already does
that dirtying, as do most of the other places
that use GUP with FOLL_WRITE.

A number of places use unpin_user_pages_dirty(_lock)
to get the pages marked dirty at unpin time, after
the data has been written into the pages.

However, there seem to be some places in the
kernel that are not marking pages dirty when
they write after GUP with FOLL_WRITE.

I suppose we need to fix those, given how
sometimes they can pin pages for a long time,
and do multiple writes over a long period of
time?

I'm combing through the tree now to find those
places.

This raises the question whether we want to
call mark_folio_dirty() at all from inside
GUP.

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary: Reviewer John Hubbard noted that follow_page_pte_commit() sets folios and pages dirty, which should be done as part of filesystem-coordinated steps to avoid problems when the page is unexpectedly dirty.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Rik,

You have delved too deep, and now uncovered something that's been
a problem for the whole time. :)

Specifically, "no, GUP should not be setting folios nor pages
dirty", because that generally needs to be done as part of a filesystem
coordinated set of steps. If the page is dirty, and the filesystem
didn't expect it to be, that leads to problems.

This is part of the big, remaining set of required fixes, that
launched the creation of pin_user_pages*() and related. Connecting
up the filesystems properly is yet to be done. And until then, this
is a real defect.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

I found about two dozen places where drivers

I'll get out patches for that, unless there's

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary:
reviewer noted that marking a page dirty in follow_page_pte_commit() can lead to issues with file system coordination, and suggested this as another problem beyond the initial concern about splitting the function

Reviewer John Hubbard pointed out a technical issue where marking a file-backed page dirty is not allowed after other preparation steps have been run, citing ext4's documentation and its own workaround using folio_set_checked(). He noted that the current implementation of unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() is also in an awkward state.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, I agree about that problem, but it's not the only one. It turns
out that the only thing worse than failing to mark a page dirty is
marking it dirty without coordinating with the filesystem.

---

Well...on a file-backed page, marking it dirty is the *last* step of
a sequence, and a driver cannot run the earlier steps.

ext4_page_mkwrite() into ext4_block_page_mkwrite() runs it in this
order:

	sb_start_pagefault(inode->i_sb);	/* freeze protection */
	file_update_time(vma->vm_file);
	filemap_invalidate_lock_shared(mapping);	/* truncate */
	ext4_journal_start(inode, EXT4_HT_WRITE_PAGE, credits);
	ext4_block_write_begin(handle, folio, 0, len, get_block);
	folio_mark_dirty(folio);
	ext4_journal_stop(handle);
	folio_wait_stable(folio);

A set_page_dirty() at the driver's write site is that
folio_mark_dirty(), but with none of the preparation above it.

ext4 documents this case already, in ext4_journalled_dirty_folio() on
the data=journal path:

  * ... except for the case when someone
  * had the page pinned and dirtied the page through this pin (e.g. by doing
  * direct IO to it). In that case we'd need to attach buffers here to the
  * transaction but we cannot due to lock ordering.

Its workaround is folio_set_checked(), which defers the real work to
ext4_writepages(). If ext4 can't do the preparation from inside the
dirty call, a driver can't either.

So for a file-backed page there's nothing the driver can add. What's
missing is a way for the filesystem to be told before the device
writes, and to revoke the pin when it needs to, which is where the
lease proposals come in. None of that exists today.

And yes, unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() is in the same awkward mess.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 4/8] mm/gup: break out follow_one_pte() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out a helper function called `follow_one_pte()` from the existing `follow_page_pte()` function in the Linux kernel's memory management code. The new helper function resolves one present PTE to the page it maps, returning no page and no error when the PTE cannot be followed but the caller may fault it in, or a negative errno when the caller must report the failure. This change is intended to simplify the `follow_page_pte()` function by reducing its complexity and making it easier to maintain. The patch does not introduce any functional changes and only modifies the code structure.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 5/8] mm/gup: fill the pages array outside the pud/pmd lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the huge page handling in the Linux kernel's memory management code to fill the pages array and flush caches outside of the pud/pmd lock. This is done by storing the page reference before unlocking, allowing the fill operation to occur safely without holding the lock. The changes are intended to be functional-equivalent to the original behavior, with no expected performance or correctness impact.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 6/8] mm/gup: return a huge page's full count from follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the Linux kernel's mm/gup module to return the full count of huge pages instead of just a mask. The changes also simplify the code by removing unnecessary variables and loops, and add an explicit check for the -EEXIST path when pages are NULL. The patch does not change the behavior of follow_page_pte(), which still returns at most 1 page.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 7/8] mm/gup: walk multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `follow_page_pte` function to walk multiple PTEs in a single call, reducing the number of page-table descents and lock acquisitions. This improves performance by eliminating redundant work for adjacent pages from different folios or plain base pages with no folio relationship. The patch was measured to reduce median get time by 2-3 times on various test cases.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 8/8] mm/gup: batch contiguous same-folio PTEs into one refcount grab
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of large memory folios (mTHP) by batching contiguous PTEs into a single refcount grab, reducing the number of try_grab_folio() calls and improving performance. The patch introduces a new function follow_pte_batch() that scans for additional PTEs to be included in a batch, and modifies the follow_page_pte_commit() function to use this batching approach. This results in significant performance improvements, with a 12.8x reduction in execution time for large mTHP folios.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves the performance of follow_page_mask() by allowing it to batch lookups and reduce lock contention. The current implementation walks the page tables one page at a time, even when contiguous pages are requested. This series changes follow_page_mask() to return a count and an array of pages, instead of a single struct page, enabling more efficient handling of large folios. Patches 1-4 prepare for this change by refactoring and splitting existing functions. Patch 5 optimizes huge page paths, patch 6 simplifies the handling of subpages, and patches 7 and 8 implement batched lookups and refcount batching, respectively. The series includes benchmark results showing a significant performance improvement.

>>
>> This is part of the big, remaining set of required fixes, that
>> launched the creation of pin_user_pages*() and related. Connecting
>> up the filesystems properly is yet to be done. And until then, this
>> is a real defect.
>>
> Not just filesystems.
> 
> I found about two dozen places where drivers
> fail to mark a page dirty after writing to
> it, after obtaining the page from GUP.
> 

Yes, I agree about that problem, but it's not the only one. It turns
out that the only thing worse than failing to mark a page dirty is
marking it dirty without coordinating with the filesystem.

> I'll get out patches for that, unless there's
> some reason I shouldn't.
> 

Well...on a file-backed page, marking it dirty is the *last* step of
a sequence, and a driver cannot run the earlier steps.

ext4_page_mkwrite() into ext4_block_page_mkwrite() runs it in this
order:

	sb_start_pagefault(inode->i_sb);	/* freeze protection */
	file_update_time(vma->vm_file);
	filemap_invalidate_lock_shared(mapping);	/* truncate */
	ext4_journal_start(inode, EXT4_HT_WRITE_PAGE, credits);
	ext4_block_write_begin(handle, folio, 0, len, get_block);
	folio_mark_dirty(folio);
	ext4_journal_stop(handle);
	folio_wait_stable(folio);

A set_page_dirty() at the driver's write site is that
folio_mark_dirty(), but with none of the preparation above it.

ext4 documents this case already, in ext4_journalled_dirty_folio() on
the data=journal path:

  * ... except for the case when someone
  * had the page pinned and dirtied the page through this pin (e.g. by doing
  * direct IO to it). In that case we'd need to attach buffers here to the
  * transaction but we cannot due to lock ordering.

Its workaround is folio_set_checked(), which defers the real work to
ext4_writepages(). If ext4 can't do the preparation from inside the
dirty call, a driver can't either.

So for a file-backed page there's nothing the driver can add. What's
missing is a way for the filesystem to be told before the device
writes, and to revoke the pin when it needs to, which is where the
lease proposals come in. None of that exists today.

And yes, unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() is in the same awkward mess.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] memcg: move LRU size accounting on reparenting instead of copying it

version_history.subject: [PATCH] memcg: move LRU size accounting on reparenting instead of copying it

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a memory accounting issue in Linux's memory cgroup (memcg) system, where the LRU size is copied instead of moved when a memory cgroup is reparented to its parent. This leads to stale values being left on the child cgroup and incorrect scans being performed by the vmscan system. The patch moves the LRU size accounting to occur during reparenting, ensuring that the parent cgroup is credited with the correct number of folios. This fix also addresses a related issue with the unevictable LRU list.
